title: What should you ask first in a cost or operations case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a cost and operations case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Cost and operations cases are about doing the same work for less, or doing it better. Here is where to start.
body:
The first question to ask

Goal: lower cost, more capacity, or reliability?

How to build your structure

  1. Map the cost base: what are the biggest lines?
  2. Benchmark each line against peers to find the biggest gap
  3. Start with the biggest gap
  4. List levers: people, process, technology, suppliers
  5. Check what each cut would do to revenue and quality

The trap most people fall into

Cutting costs that carry revenue.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the cost reduction framework.

Two prompts to try

A hospital's emergency waiting times have doubled in a year.

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Number of arrivals, by hour and day; Case mix: older, sicker patients take longer
  • Capacity: Doctors and nurses on shift vs arrivals; Cubicles and beds in the department
  • Process inside the department: Triage, tests, waiting for a specialist; Handovers between shifts
  • Flow out: Waiting for a ward bed upstairs; Discharges and social care delays

Where to start: Flow out: in most hospitals, patients waiting for a ward bed block the emergency department.

The trap: Only asking for more staff without checking whether patients are stuck waiting for beds.

A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show a model structure
  • Number of returns: Online orders: did sales grow?; Return rate by category, size, brand; serial returners
  • Cost per return: Shipping, handling, refurbishing; Items that can no longer be sold
  • Why customers return: Fit and sizing, photos and descriptions; Ordering several sizes on purpose
  • Policy: Free returns, return window; Charging, store returns, exchanges first

Where to start: Orders × return rate × cost per return: find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: Listing policies to change without first splitting the number of returns from cost per return.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation. Practise this case type in the free casebook: every case has a worked answer.
